learn.title: The DOM pattern (every exercise is this)
learn.text: Almost every web exercise is the same 4 steps: 1) get the elements, 2) listen for an event, 3) read something (input value, event, data), 4) change the page. If you are stuck, say which step you are stuck on.

learn.title: Selecting elements
learn.text: getElementById returns ONE element (or null). querySelector takes a CSS selector and returns the FIRST match. querySelectorAll returns ALL matches (a list you can forEach over).
learn.code:
document.getElementById('list')        // <ul id="list">
document.querySelector('.item')        // first element with class item
document.querySelector('#list li')     // first li inside #list
document.querySelectorAll('.item')     // every .item
  .forEach(el => console.log(el.textContent));

learn.title: Changing the page
learn.text: textContent sets plain text (safe). innerHTML parses HTML (dangerous with user/API text because it can run injected HTML). classList add/remove/toggle is how you change styling from JS. remove() deletes an element.

learn.title: Events and forms
learn.text: A form submit reloads the page by default. event.preventDefault() stops that. Use the 'submit' event on the form, not 'click' on the button, so the Enter key works too.

learn.title: Arrays and objects
learn.text: map makes a new array by transforming each item. filter keeps items where the function returns true. find returns the first match. forEach just loops (returns nothing). some/every return true/false.

learn.title: fetch, async/await, try/catch (Exercise 4)
learn.text: fetch is asynchronous: it returns a Promise. 'await' pauses the function until the Promise is done, and can only be used inside a function marked 'async'. You await TWICE: once for the response, once for response.json(). Wrap it in try/catch so network errors don't crash.

learn.title: localStorage (search history)
learn.text: localStorage only stores strings. So objects/arrays must be turned into text with JSON.stringify when saving and back with JSON.parse when loading. getItem returns null if the key doesn't exist, hence the || [].

learn.title: Comparison traps
learn.text: Use === (strict) not ==. '5' + 3 is '53' (string concat) but '5' - 3 is 2. An empty string, 0, null, undefined and NaN are all falsy, which is why `if (!term)` works for empty input.

0 == '0'       // true  (avoid ==)
0 === '0'      // false
'5' + 3        // '53'
'5' - 3        // 2
typeof null    // 'object' (a famous quirk)
if (!'') { /* runs: empty string is falsy */ }

learn.title: Internet vs. the Web
learn.text: The Internet is the network infrastructure: computers connected with the TCP/IP protocol (started as ARPANET, 1983). The Web is ONE application built on top of the Internet: hypertext documents and other resources identified by URLs, linked by hyperlinks. Other Internet applications: email, FTP, telnet. Tim Berners-Lee created the Web (1989) by developing/joining three technologies: URL (address of a resource), HTML (structure of content), HTTP (communication protocol).

learn.title: How the Web evolved
learn.text: 1990s: static pages. GET fetches pages, forms are sent with POST, every request refreshes the whole page, logic only on the server. Late 1990s: dynamic pages generated on the server per request (PHP, ASP) with cookies and databases, still full page reloads. 2000s: AJAX (XMLHttpRequest): JavaScript asks the server for pieces of data without reloading the page. Today: SPA (Single Page Application): the browser loads the app once, most logic runs on the client, the server mainly stores data and handles authentication.

learn.text: The client sends a request, the server sends a response. A server is a machine (physical or virtual in the cloud) AND the program that provides the service; it has a known address (DNS name resolves to an IP) and listens on a port (web servers: 80 by default). Examples: Apache, Nginx, Microsoft IIS, Node.js. Clients: browsers (content is HTML, CSS, JavaScript) and native mobile apps (Android: Java/Kotlin, iOS: Swift).

MIME type = 'type/subtype' describing the resource.

Validation attributes: required, pattern (regex), min, max. Radio buttons = exclusive choice (same name); checkboxes = non-exclusive. select > option = drop-down; textarea = multi-line text; button type = button | reset | submit.

learn.title: CSS basics: syntax and three ways to add CSS
learn.text: HTML = content, CSS = style and layout. A rule = selector + { property: value; }. Three ways: INLINE (style attribute, one element only), INTERNAL (<style> in the head, whole page), EXTERNAL (separate .css file linked with <link rel="stylesheet">, reusable by many pages, separates content from presentation). Every tag has browser default styles; your rules override them.
learn.code:
body { /* selector */ color: red; /* property: value */ }

learn.title: Selectors
learn.text: Type selector p (by tag). Class selector .myClass. ID selector #myId. Combined p.myClass (a p WITH class myClass). Grouping h1, h2 (both). Descendant nav li (li at any depth inside nav). Child ul > li (only direct children). Adjacent sibling h1 + p (the p immediately after an h1). Pseudo-class a:hover (element state: :hover, :focus, :visited, :first-child). Universal * (all tags).

learn.title: The cascade: importance, specificity, order
learn.text: When several rules target the same element the cascade picks ONE result using three levels. 1) Origin and importance: !important > inline > internal > external > browser default. 2) Specificity: inline > id > class/pseudo-class/attribute > element/pseudo-element. 3) Source order: with equal specificity, the rule defined LATER wins. Inheritance: many properties (like color) pass from parent to children unless a more specific rule on the child overrides them.
learn.code: body { color: blue; } /* all text blue... */ h1 { color: red; } /* ...but h1 is red (more specific than inherited) */ p { color: red; } /* element */ .note { color: green; } /* class beats element */ #intro { color: blue; } /* id beats class */

learn.title: Text, fonts, backgrounds, borders
learn.text: text-align: center|left|right|justify. text-decoration: none removes link underlines (shorthand for line, color, style). font-size: 1em = the current font size (default 16px), so 40px = 2.5em. font-family lists fallbacks ending with a generic family (serif, sans-serif, monospace). Google Fonts: link in head + font-family in CSS. background-image, background-repeat (repeat default, no-repeat), background-size (cover fills and may crop; contain fits inside), background-position, background-clip (border-box default). border: width style color; border-radius rounds corners.

learn.title: Box model, display, position
learn.text: Box model, from the inside out: content, padding (space inside the border), border, margin (space outside the border). margin: 100px 40px 20px 30px = top right bottom left. display: none (not shown), inline, block, inline-block (inline but accepts width/height), flex, grid. position: static (default, normal flow), relative (offset from its normal place), absolute (relative to a positioned ancestor), fixed (stays in place when scrolling).

learn.title: Flexbox and responsive design
learn.text: display:flex on a container makes its children flex items. flex-direction (row, column...), flex-wrap, justify-content (main axis: flex-start, center, space-between...), align-items (cross axis). On an item, flex: 1 means an equal share; flex: 2 means twice as much. Media queries (@media) apply rules only under conditions like viewport width; they only work correctly if the HTML has the viewport meta tag.

learn.title: Why version control, and what Git is
learn.text: Version control avoids (a) many versions of a project in different files and (b) overwriting the same file with no history. Git was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage development of the Linux kernel. A Git repository is a .git/ folder inside your project folder; it tracks every change to the files and builds a history over time. A GitHub profile can work as a portfolio.
learn.code:
mkdir mynewproject     # new folder
cd mynewproject        # go into it
git init               # now the folder is a Git repository (.git/ created)

learn.title: Local workflow and the three areas
learn.text: Working directory = where you edit files. Staging area = where you prepare the changes for the next commit. Local repository = the code that has been committed (snapshots). Remote repository = the server used for sharing and collaboration (e.g. GitHub). A file can be unmodified, modified or staged. git status shows the state of the working directory and staging area. git add moves changes to the staging area. git commit -m saves a snapshot of everything staged into the local repository. git log / git log --oneline shows history; each commit has a unique identifier (SHA-1).
learn.code:
git status                      # what is going on?
git add .                       # working directory -> staging area (all files)
git commit -m "First version"   # staging area -> local repository
git log --oneline               # history, one line per commit

Working Directory --add--> Staging Area --commit--> Local Repo --push--> Remote Repo
                  <-restore-                         <-fetch / pull-

learn.title: Commit messages and .gitignore
learn.text: A good commit message describes WHAT was changed and WHY, so you can identify that version later (conventions like 'chore: ...', 'feat: ...'). .gitignore lists files that must not be tracked or made public later (e.g. *.pem, *.log, passwords.txt, node_modules/). git add . stages all files in the directory, including ones you did not want. Once a file is already tracked, .gitignore alone does not help: you must untrack it manually. Set up .gitignore BEFORE the first commit.
learn.code:
# .gitignore
*.pem
*.log
passwords.txt
node_modules/

git commit -m "feat: add contact form"
git commit -m "chore: ignore node_modules"

learn.title: Git vs. GitHub, and working with a remote
learn.text: git = version control tool that works locally. GitHub = cloud-based platform for hosting repositories and collaboration (others: GitLab, Bitbucket, Codeberg). Configure who authors your commits with git config user.name / user.email; priority: --local (project) > --global (user) > --system. git remote add origin <url> links a local project to a remote. git push sends committed changes from the current branch to the remote. git pull gets data from the remote: git pull = git fetch + git merge (fetch downloads remote changes without changing your working files). git clone downloads an existing repository.
learn.code:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

git remote add origin https://github.com/your-username/your-repo-name.git
git push -u origin main      # send my commits
git pull                     # = git fetch + git merge
git clone https://github.com/twbs/bootstrap.git

learn.title: Tags, Releases and GitHub Pages
learn.text: A tag marks a specific commit as a named version (releases, milestones, stable versions). A GitHub Release = a tag + a description + downloadable files; users can download it as a ZIP without needing Git. GitHub Pages publishes the files in a repository as a webpage at myuser.github.io/myrepository.
learn.code:

git push origin v1-html      # push the tag to GitHub
git tag                      # list all tags

learn.title: Branching and merging
learn.text: Branches enable isolated feature work, are safer than working directly on main, and let people collaborate without overwriting each other's work. To integrate: switch to main, then merge the feature branch into it. git switch is only for switching branches; git restore is for restoring files; the older git checkout does both.
learn.code:
git branch                    # list branches
git branch name_of_branch     # create a branch
git switch name_of_branch     # switch to it
git switch -c name_of_branch  # create AND switch
git branch -d name_of_branch  # delete (clean up after merge)

git switch -c add-image       # 1. create branch and switch
git add .   ;   git commit -m "Add real image"   # 2. work on the branch
git switch main               # 3. back to main
git merge add-image           # 4. merge feature into main

learn.title: Clone vs. fork, and pull requests
learn.text: clone copies a repo to YOUR COMPUTER (a local copy); use it to get a working copy or to work on a repo where you already have access (e.g. download your own repo). fork makes a REMOTE copy of someone's repo under your own GitHub account; use it when you don't have permission to push to the original, you want your own writable copy on GitHub, or you want to contribute back with a pull request. Pull request workflow: fork -> clone your fork -> create a branch -> commit and push to your fork -> open a pull request against the original -> review and discussion -> maintainers merge. Collaborators are added in the repository's Settings.
learn.code:
fork -> clone -> branch -> commit & push -> pull request -> review -> merge

clone = remote copy -> my computer
fork  = someone's repo -> my GitHub account

learn.title: When things go wrong: the mindset
learn.text: 1) Run git status, always start there. 2) Identify your current branch. 3) Ask: is the problem local, branch-related, or remote? 4) Read the error message carefully. 5) Do not force-push or delete anything unless you know why.
learn.code: git status      # always the first step

learn.title: Merge conflict and rejected push
learn.text: MERGE CONFLICT: two branches changed the same lines in the same file differently, so Git cannot decide and stops. The file contains markers <<<<<<< HEAD, =======, >>>>>>> branch_name. Conflicts are normal. Fix: git status (see conflicted files), open the file, choose which version to keep (or combine), remove ALL markers, save, git add <file>, git commit. PUSH REJECTED (non-fast-forward, 'remote contains work that you do not have locally'): someone else pushed first (or you edited on GitHub), so your branch is behind. Fix: git pull, resolve conflicts if they appear, git push. Do NOT git push --force and do not delete your local repo.
learn.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
<title>Sherlock</title>          <- my version (current branch)
=======
<title>Holmes</title>            <- the other branch's version
>>>>>>> add-title

# resolve: keep one/combine, delete the 3 marker lines, then
git add index.html
git commit -m "resolve merge conflict"

# push rejected:
git pull        # then fix any conflict
git push

learn.title: Wrong branch, detached HEAD, tracked files, authentication
learn.text: WRONG BRANCH, not pushed: git reset --soft HEAD~1 (undo last commit, changes stay staged), git stash, git switch correct-branch, git stash pop, git add ., git commit. Already pushed: git switch -c new-branch, git push -u origin new-branch, git switch main, git log --oneline (find the commit id), git revert <commit-id>, git push. DETACHED HEAD: you checked out a specific commit, not a branch; to just look, git switch main; to keep changes, git switch -c new-branch-name; don't commit there without a branch. ACCIDENTALLY TRACKED FILES: git rm --cached <file> (or -r <folder>), add it to .gitignore, git add .gitignore, git commit, git push. The file stays in history: clutter = fine; secrets you can change (API keys, passwords) = rotate them immediately; sensitive data you cannot change = remove from history (git filter-repo or BFG, force-push, notify the team). AUTHENTICATION: GitHub no longer accepts account passwords; use a Personal Access Token, SSH keys, or VS Code's Source Control. Never commit tokens or keys.
learn.code:
# wrong branch (not pushed)
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git stash
git switch correct-branch
git stash pop
git add .
git commit -m "your message"

# stop tracking a file but keep it locally
git rm --cached <filename>
echo "node_modules/" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "chore: ignore node_modules"

learn.title: Web accessibility and the POUR principles
learn.text: Accessibility = making websites usable for ALL people, including those with visual, auditory, motor or cognitive disabilities. It benefits everyone: better contrast helps in bright sunlight, captions help in noisy places, keyboard navigation helps people who prefer keyboards. Why it matters: legal requirements (WCAG = Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, the EU accessibility act), social responsibility (equal access), and practical benefits (usability, SEO = search engine optimization, user experience). The four principles (POUR): Perceivable (information must be visible or audible), Operable (usable with mouse, keyboard or assistive tech), Understandable (content and navigation are clear), Robust (works with different devices and assistive technologies).

Accessibility features:
- text alternatives for images (alt attribute)
- high colour contrast between text and background
- captions or transcripts for videos
- keyboard navigation (tabbing through links and forms)

learn.title: Role of JavaScript
learn.text: The client technologies: HTML = structure, CSS = style, JavaScript = interaction. JavaScript runs in two environments. In the BROWSER (client-side): reacts to user actions (clicks, typing, scrolling), updates the page without reloading it (showing/hiding content, form validation, animations, a like counter). On the SERVER (server-side, e.g. with Node.js): handles data that must be stored or kept secure, business logic and databases (saving accounts, payments, sending emails). JavaScript is NOT Java: they are different languages. The browser gives JavaScript several APIs: the DOM (modify the HTML page; the focus of this course), Canvas/WebGL graphics, audio/video, geolocation, storage, notifications. Add JS to a page with <script src="file.js"></script> or code inside <script> tags.
learn.code:

<script>
  // code written directly in the page
</script>

learn.title: Variables and primitive types
learn.text: You do not declare a type; JavaScript infers it. var is the old way. let declares a variable with reduced scope (only inside its block, the curly braces). const declares a constant that cannot be reassigned. let and const are preferred over var, because the reduced scope prevents accidental bugs. Primitive types: Number (integers and decimals), String (text in ' ', " " or backticks for template literals), Boolean (true/false), Undefined (declared but not assigned; the default), Null (intentional absence of any object value).
learn.code:
const hasShorthair = true;   // constant, cannot be changed
let weight = 4.3;            // like var but block-scoped
let name = "Toast";          // String
let isSleeping = true;       // Boolean
let owner;                   // undefined (declared, no value)
let previousOwner = null;    // null (intentionally empty)
`Hello ${name}`           // template literal

learn.title: Objects and arrays
learn.text: An object is a collection of key-value pairs, read with dot notation. Shorthand: if key and variable name match you can write { catName, catAge }. An array is an ordered list: index starts at 0, .length is the size, push adds to the END, pop removes the LAST. for...of loops over the values. map transforms each item into a new array; filter keeps the items for which the function returns true.

learn.title: Functions and arrow functions
learn.text: A function is a reusable block of code that can take input, process it and return output. Traditional syntax: function greetCat(name) { return ... }. Arrow function syntax (ES6): const greetCat = (name) => { return ... }. Arrow shorthand: no braces and no return keyword; the expression is returned automatically. With curly braces you need an explicit return. Three patterns: no input (always the same), uses an outer variable (tied to it), takes a parameter (flexible and reusable). Arrow functions appear often with arrays (map) and event listeners. console.log() prints to the browser console.

learn.title: Operators and control flow
learn.text: Arithmetic: + - * / % (remainder) ** (exponent). Assignment: = += -= *= /=. Comparison: == (loose: 5 == "5" is true), === (strict: 5 === "5" is false), !=, !==, <, >, <=, >=. Logical: && (and), || (or), ! (not). Conditions: if / else if / else. Ternary: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse (assign a value based on a condition in one expression). switch checks multiple cases (with break and default); an object lookup is a common alternative. Loops: while, for, for...of (values of an array), for...in (keys of an object).
learn.code:
let sum = 5 + 3;      // 8
let power = 2 ** 3;   // 8
let totalCats = 2;  totalCats += 3;   // 5
5 == "5"    // true  (loose)
5 === "5"   // false (strict)
true && false   // false
true || false   // true

if (catAge < 1) { console.log("Kitten"); }
else if (catAge < 10) { console.log("Adult"); }
else { console.log("Senior"); }

let ageGroup = (age >= 2) ? "Adult" : "Young";

for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { console.log(i); }       // 0..4
for (let cat of cats) { console.log(cat); }            // values
for (let key in cat) { console.log(key, cat[key]); }   // keys

learn.title: More array methods
learn.text: Finding: find (first match), findIndex (index of the first match), includes (true/false). Checking: every (all match?), some (any match?). Transforming: join, reverse, sort. Aggregating: reduce. Careful: sort() with no function sorts values as TEXT, so numbers come out in the wrong order; give it a compare function (a, b) => a - b for numbers. sort and reverse change the original array, so sort a copy with [...cats].sort().
learn.code:
cats.find(cat => cat.length > 5);        // "Naranja" (first match)
cats.findIndex(cat => cat.length > 5);   // 1
cats.includes("Toast");                  // true
cats.every(cat => cat.length > 3);       // true (all?)
cats.some(cat => cat === "Toast");       // true (any?)
cats.join(", ");                         // "Toast, Naranja, Kinsky"
[...cats].sort();                        // alphabetical, on a copy
[3, 4, 5, 6].reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0);   // 18

let myNumbers = [21, 4, 30, 100000, 1];
myNumbers.sort((a, b) => a - b);         // [1, 4, 21, 30, 100000]

learn.title: The DOM API: selecting elements
learn.text: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the JavaScript API provided by the browser to manipulate the page's HTML. First select the element. getElementById: one element by its id. getElementsByClassName: all elements with a class (an HTMLCollection). getElementsByTagName: all elements of a tag (an HTMLCollection). querySelector: the FIRST element matching a CSS selector. querySelectorAll: ALL elements matching a CSS selector (a NodeList).
learn.code:
document.getElementById('container');
document.getElementsByClassName('myClass');    // HTMLCollection
document.getElementsByTagName('p');            // HTMLCollection
document.querySelector('nav > ul > .first');   // first match
document.querySelectorAll('div > p');          // NodeList (all matches)

learn.title: The DOM API: changing, creating, removing elements
learn.text: Change in three ways: content, attributes, appearance. Content: textContent (plain text) and innerHTML (HTML inside). Attributes: setAttribute, getAttribute, removeAttribute. Appearance: classList.add / remove / toggle, and style (e.g. element.style.color = 'blue'). Create: createElement makes a new element; appendChild adds it as the LAST child of another element. Remove: remove() removes the element itself; removeChild removes a child from its parent.

learn.title: Event listeners
learn.text: Events make pages interactive: clicks, key presses, form submissions... addEventListener takes the type of interaction and a function that says what happens after it. Common events: change (an element changed), click, mouseover, mouseout, keydown (a key is pressed), load (the page has finished loading). For keyboard events the function receives an event object; event.key says which key. Typical patterns: get the elements, attach a listener, and inside it change content, classes or styles.

learn.title: Kažigram with JavaScript (what concepts it uses)
learn.text: const/let store form inputs and post data. Array methods manage the list of posts. Event listeners on submit handle the form. createElement + appendChild add new post cards to the page. classList.toggle switches the like button (heart icon). textContent updates the like count. remove() deletes a post. Conceptual examples: a chat app (new message = createElement + textContent + appendChild; send button or Enter keydown listener; classList for mine vs theirs) and a snake game (keydown listener, event.key for the arrow, style to move, textContent for points).
learn.code:
form submit   -> addEventListener('submit', ...)
new post card -> createElement + appendChild
like button   -> classList.toggle + textContent
delete post   -> remove()

learn.title: Why use third-party JavaScript libraries
learn.text: Why not reinvent the wheel? Faster development, well-documented solutions, battle-tested code, bug fixes and maintenance, browser quirks handled, and a large user base. Libraries exist at different layers: CSS layer (styling and animation: Bootstrap, Tailwind CSS, Animate.css); JS + DOM layer (interaction and data: the focus here); component framework layer (application structure: React, Angular, Vue.js); development tools (Vite, npm, ESLint, Babel).
learn.code:
CSS layer:        Bootstrap, Tailwind CSS, Animate.css
JS + DOM layer:   GSAP, Flatpickr, Toastify, Chart.js ...
Frameworks:       React, Angular, Vue.js
Dev tools:        Vite, npm, ESLint, Babel

learn.title: What tasks libraries handle
learn.text: Six common tasks. DOM manipulation: vanilla JS (getElementById, querySelector, textContent, createElement, appendChild, remove) for small projects; component frameworks (React, Angular, Vue) update the DOM through a Virtual DOM (you describe what the UI should look like, the framework works out what to change); historically jQuery. Form validation: HTML attributes (required, pattern, min, max, type="email"), custom JS with addEventListener, libraries Yup and Validator.js, Formik and React Hook Form in React, Survey.js for survey builders. Animations and transitions: CSS transitions/keyframes/Animate.css, and JS libraries GSAP and Anime.js for complex programmatic animations CSS cannot do. Advanced interactions: Flatpickr (date/time pickers), Toastify (toast = temporary notifications), Cropper.js (image editing), Quill.js (rich text editor), Sortable.js (drag and drop), Three.js (3D graphics). Data visualization: Chart.js (bar, line, pie, doughnut), Recharts (charts as React components), Cytoscape.js (network diagrams). UI component interactions (menus, accordions, tabs, modals, carts, form wizards): vanilla JS for simple cases, frameworks like Angular, Vue, React for complex ones.
learn.code:
Animations    -> GSAP, Anime.js
Date picker   -> Flatpickr
Notifications -> Toastify (toast = temporary message)
Charts        -> Chart.js (React: Recharts)
Validation    -> Yup, Validator.js (React: Formik, React Hook Form)

learn.title: How you use a library: CDN + find the element + call a function
learn.text: A library is loaded from a CDN: a <script src> for the JavaScript (and a <link rel="stylesheet"> if it has CSS, like Flatpickr and Toastify) in the head. The JS file provides the functions. Then your code finds the element and calls the library function. GSAP: gsap.fromTo(element, startValues, endValues) animates, e.g. scale 1 to 1.4 with yoyo and repeat so it grows and shrinks back. Flatpickr: flatpickr('#dateRange', { mode: 'range', dateFormat: 'Y-m-d' }) turns a text input into a date range picker. In the GSAP like button, liked = !liked toggles a boolean, classList.toggle('liked') switches between class 'like-btn' and 'like-btn liked', and the count goes up or down with likes += liked ? 1 : -1.
learn.code:
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/gsap@3.12/dist/gsap.min.js"></script>

btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
  liked = !liked;                       // toggle the boolean
  likes += liked ? 1 : -1;
  btn.textContent = liked ? '♥' : '♡';
  btn.classList.toggle('liked');
  countEl.textContent = likes + ' likes';
  gsap.fromTo(btn, { scale: 1 }, { scale: 1.4, duration: 0.15, yoyo: true, repeat: 1 });
});

flatpickr("#dateRange", { mode: "range", dateFormat: "Y-m-d" });

learn.title: Library examples: Toastify and Chart.js
learn.text: Toastify: load its CSS (<link>) and JS (<script src>) from a CDN, then call Toastify({ ... }).showToast(). The options object has text (the message), duration (milliseconds) and style. In the form example: preventDefault stops the page reload, the caption is read from the textarea, a toast shows 'Post published: ...', and this.reset() clears the form. Chart.js: load the JS from a CDN, put a <canvas> in the page, select it and get its drawing context with getContext('2d'), then create the chart with new Chart(ctx, { type, data }). type = chart type (bar, line, pie...), data.labels = the labels for the X-axis, datasets[].data = the values for the Y-axis, plus label, backgroundColor, borderColor, borderWidth. Other libraries worth knowing: Quill.js (rich text editors), Cropper.js (image cropping), Survey.js (surveys and forms), Three.js (3D graphics), Cytoscape.js (network diagrams), Phaser (2D game engine), Sortable.js (drag and drop).

learn.title: Asynchronous JavaScript: why it matters
learn.text: addEventListener, textContent, classList.toggle run instantly. But fetching data from a server can take 1-5 seconds. WITHOUT async: JavaScript waits for the data, the page freezes and the user cannot interact. WITH async: JavaScript starts the fetch and continues running other code, returns to the data when ready, and the page stays responsive. Main uses: sending a form (payment, posting a photo), sending messages, using third-party REST APIs, any communication with a server. JavaScript is single-threaded (unlike Java threads it does not run code in parallel); an event loop manages tasks so the page stays responsive. Analogy: asynchronous = ordering food and doing other things while waiting; synchronous = standing in a queue doing nothing.
learn.code:
sync (blocking):  start request ....... wait (page frozen) ....... use data
async:            start request -> keep running other code -> come back when data is ready

learn.title: Callbacks, Promises, async/await (a progression)
learn.text: Three ways of dealing with asynchrony, each solving problems of the previous one. 1) CALLBACKS: a function passed as an argument to another function, called when the asynchronous task is done, not immediately. addEventListener and setTimeout use callbacks. Problem: deeply nested callbacks, hard to read and debug, with error handling repeated at every level. 2) PROMISES: a Promise represents the eventual result of an async operation; states: pending, then fulfilled or rejected. Chain .then() steps and use ONE .catch() for the whole chain. Problem: if steps need each other's data you must keep it in outer variables. 3) ASYNC/AWAIT: the modern standard, built on top of Promises, reads like regular sequential code: all variables stay in the same scope and one try/catch handles the errors.

learn.title: async/await rules
learn.text: Define the function with async. Use await before the slow operation (it pauses THAT function until the Promise is done while the rest of the page continues normally). Wrap it in try/catch for error handling (like Java). Both function syntaxes work: async function getData() {...} and const getData = async () => {...}.

learn.title: REST APIs: what they are and why we need them
learn.text: So far our JavaScript used hardcoded data. Real applications need real, up-to-date data: movie information, weather, maps, payments, anything that changes or belongs to a user. A REST API (Representational State Transfer Application Programming Interface) is an address (URL) that another server provides. How it works: 1) our JavaScript sends an HTTP request to that URL; 2) the server processes it; 3) the server responds with data in JSON format; 4) we use the data to update the DOM. Fetching uses async/await because waiting for a server response takes time. Examples: OpenStreetMap/Nominatim (maps), REST Countries, OpenSky Network (flights), Open Library (books), Wikipedia API, OMDB (movies).
learn.code: JS --HTTP request--> URL of the API (server) --JSON response--> JS --> update the DOM

learn.title: Resources, HTTP methods, JSON, statelessness
learn.text: Data is a RESOURCE identified by a unique URL; the HTTP METHOD says what you want to do with it. GET = retrieve ('give me the list of books'), POST = create ('add this new book'), PUT = update ('change this book's information'), DELETE = remove. Pattern: URL identifies the resource, HTTP method defines the action. Data format: REST APIs typically respond with JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), which looks like a JavaScript object. JSON is preferred over XML because it is lighter and directly compatible with JavaScript objects. STATELESSNESS: each request must be independent and contain all the information the server needs; the server does not remember previous requests or store session information. In practice every request must include authentication if needed, which is why APIs often require an API key in every request.
learn.code:
JSON:   { "name": "Toast", "age": 6, "likes": 47 }
XML:    <cat><name>Toast</name><age>6</age></cat>      (older, heavier)

GET    /books      -> list of books
POST   /books      -> add a new book
PUT    /books/1    -> update book 1
DELETE /books/1    -> remove book 1

learn.title: fetch(): GET and POST
learn.text: fetch() is the modern built-in JavaScript function for HTTP requests; used with async/await. By default it uses GET (no method needed). response.ok tells if the request succeeded; throw an Error with response.status to detect HTTP errors. response.json() extracts the JSON and needs await too. For POST (send data to the server) you must set it explicitly: method: 'POST' says it is a create request, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } tells the server the data format is JSON, body: JSON.stringify(obj) converts the JavaScript object to a JSON string.

learn.title: Kažigram with jsonbin.io
learn.text: jsonbin.io provides a simple REST API for storing JSON data. Create an account, create a bin (a storage location for JSON; each bin stores one JSON document), get the API key and the bin ID. GET retrieves the entire bin (all posts at once). PUT replaces the entire bin (send the whole updated array). The headers include the API key: statelessness in practice, every request must authenticate itself.
learn.code:
GET  bin  -> all posts at once
PUT  bin  -> replace the whole bin (send the whole updated array)
headers include the API key (every request authenticates itself)

learn.title: Exercise 3: the Todo list, step by step
learn.text: Adding a task: read the input's value, check it is not empty (if empty do nothing), createElement('li') with the task text, appendChild to the list, clear the input, update the total count. Marking completed: clicking a task toggles the 'completed' CSS class (strikethrough); clicking again removes it; the counter shows 'Remaining: X | Total: Y' where X = uncompleted tasks and Y = all tasks. Bonuses: a 'Remove last' button, a notification for empty input (Toastr/Toastify), and preventing duplicates.

learn.title: Exercise 4: movie search with fetch, step by step
learn.text: The form's submit listener: 1) preventDefault (otherwise the page reloads after submit); 2) read the value from the input; 3) clear previous results by setting innerHTML of the results element to empty; 4) build the API URL with the key and search term (http://www.omdbapi.com/?apikey=API_KEY&s=term); 5) call fetch(url) and use await to get the response; 6) call response.json() and use await to get the actual data; 7) handle empty results: OMDB returns Response: "False" when nothing is found, so show a message; 8) for each movie call createMovieCard(movie) and append the returned Bootstrap card to the results; 9) wrap steps 4-8 in try/catch to handle errors. The API key goes in config.js (const API_KEY = ...) loaded before script.js.

learn.title: Why React: the problems with direct DOM manipulation
learn.text: In JavaScript you manipulate the DOM directly (getElementById, addEventListener, querySelector). As apps grow this gets difficult: more UI elements to manage and update, hard to track which DOM parts need updating, state management across the app becomes error-prone, and code is duplicated because there is no structure for reusable parts (buttons, forms, cards). The result is 'DOM spaghetti': hard to read, test and maintain. In Kažigram, each new feature (comments, profiles, notifications, search, multiple pages) adds more getElementById, addEventListener and innerHTML, the code grows uncontrollably, the same logic is repeated, and one change breaks something else. The solution is to split the UI into independent, reusable parts: components. Each component is devoted to one specific task, receives data as input (props) and returns a user interface.

learn.title: From requirements to component design
learn.text: Process: 1) read the requirements; 2) find repeating patterns = component candidates; 3) identify what data each part needs = props candidates; 4) identify what changes over time = state candidates; 5) draw the component tree. Ask: What repeats? (each post looks the same). What changes? (like count updates). What is separate? (adding a post is its own feature). Who needs this data? (decides where state lives). Kažigram components: App (the root, holds all posts), Header (logo, navigation), PostList (renders all PostCards), PostCard (x many: photo, title, caption, like count) with LikeButton and DeleteButton, and PostForm (title, caption, image URL inputs). PostCard receives a post object as props. Does the like count need to be saved? Then App state. Only visual feedback? Component state. PostForm input values are component state. There is no single right answer; design decisions matter.
learn.code:
App
├── Header
├── PostList
│   └── PostCard (x many)
│       ├── LikeButton
│       └── DeleteButton
└── PostForm

learn.title: One-way vs. two-way data binding
learn.text: Both solve the same problem: keeping the UI in sync with the data. In both the parent owns the state; the difference is whether the child can only REQUEST changes or can sync changes back through binding. ONE-WAY binding: data flows in one direction only. The application updates the UI; the UI cannot directly update application data. The parent passes a value down, and the child emits an event/request up; the parent updates the state. Used by React (and Vue via props). TWO-WAY binding: data flows in both directions; the UI automatically updates the application data too. Used by Angular and Vue (with v-model). In React: data (props) flows DOWN from parent to child, events flow UP from child to parent; the parent decides what changes. This makes it predictable and easier to debug.
learn.code:
one-way (React):   parent state --props--> child
                   child --event/callback--> parent --updates state--> UI re-renders
two-way (Angular, Vue v-model): child edits the data directly through the binding

learn.title: What React is and its core ideas
learn.text: React is a JavaScript library for building web and native user interfaces. Popular front-end frameworks: Angular (2010/2016; full framework, TypeScript-first), React (2013; component library, virtual DOM at runtime), Vue (2014; lightweight framework), Svelte (2016; compiler-based, no virtual DOM at runtime). Core ideas: reusable components (build once, use everywhere = less duplication); Virtual DOM (React updates only what changed, not the entire page); one-way data binding (data flows down, events flow up = predictable). Virtual DOM: without React (vanilla JS) the developer decides manually which DOM element to update, which is error-prone as complexity grows. With React the developer describes what the UI should look like; React compares the new Virtual DOM with the previous one (diffing) and updates only the necessary parts automatically.
learn.code:
new Virtual DOM  --diff against-->  previous Virtual DOM
      -> React updates only the parts of the real DOM that changed

learn.title: Components and JSX
learn.text: A React component is a function that accepts props as input and returns the UI as JSX (JavaScript XML). It is independent and reusable. JSX = JavaScript + XML: HTML is a specific version of XML with fixed tags; XML lets you define your own tags, and JSX borrows that syntax so you can write your own tags (components) like <LikeButton />. A tag has a name (required), attributes and children; with no children close it with a slash. Component names start with UPPERCASE (ShoppingCart, PostCard); HTML tags are lowercase. Use className, not class (class is reserved in JavaScript). Any JavaScript EXPRESSION can go inside { } (variables, calculations, function calls, ternary operators), but not statements. Both traditional function and arrow function syntax work; arrow functions are more common. Class components exist but are no longer recommended. A component is defined in a .jsx file and exported with export default.

learn.title: Styling and conditional rendering in JSX
learn.text: Three styling options. 1) External CSS file: import './App.css' and className="card". 2) Inline style as a JavaScript object: const style = { backgroundColor: '#f0f0f0' }; <div style={style}>. 3) Direct inline with double curly braces: style={{ backgroundColor: '#f0f0f0' }}; the outer { } is the JSX expression and the inner { } is the JavaScript object. Style properties are camelCase (backgroundColor, not background-color) because it is a JavaScript object, not CSS. Conditional styling: style={{ display: props.show ? 'block' : 'none' }}. Conditional rendering: use the ternary condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse inside { }, or && to render something only when a condition is true.

learn.title: JSX is transpiled by Babel
learn.text: Browsers can only execute vanilla JavaScript, not JSX. Transpilation converts JSX to vanilla JS. Babel does it: 1) parse the JSX source into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), 2) transform the AST, 3) generate vanilla JavaScript. JSX becomes React.createElement(type, props, children). With Vite this happens automatically on save, so we never write React.createElement ourselves.
learn.code: Hello! // Babel produces: React.createElement('span', null, 'Hello!') // type props children Click Me // becomes: React.createElement(MyButton, { color: "blue" }, "Click Me")

learn.title: Starting a React project with Vite
learn.text: Old and deprecated: create-react-app. Modern frontend only (used in the course): Vite (fast dev server, HMR, production builds). Modern fullstack: Next.js (when you need server-side rendering). Install Node.js first (it comes with npm, the package manager). Then: npm create vite@latest (choose React, JavaScript, ESLint), npm install, npm run dev (dev server at http://localhost:5173/). Project structure: public/ (static files), src/ (your code: App.jsx main component, main.jsx React entry point, App.css component styles, index.css global styles), index.html (the only HTML file), package.json (dependencies and scripts), vite.config.js (development configuration), .gitignore, README.md. package.json scripts: npm run dev (start the dev server), npm run build (create production files), npm run lint (check code quality), npm run preview. dependencies are used in production (react, react-dom, which connects React to the browser DOM); devDependencies only during development (vite, eslint, @vitejs/plugin-react). HMR (Hot Module Replacement) swaps, adds or removes modules while the app is running without reloading the page: only the changed module is recreated and you don't lose the current application state.
learn.code:
npm create vite@latest      # choose React + JavaScript
npm install
npm run dev                 # http://localhost:5173/
npm run build               # production files

Setup chain:
Node.js (runs JS outside the browser, includes npm)
 -> npm (package manager, installs React, Vite...)
 -> Vite (dev server + build tool, uses Babel internally)
 -> React + Babel
We write JSX -> Vite serves -> Babel transpiles to vanilla JS -> browser runs JS

learn.title: Creating components, rendering lists, DevTools
learn.text: Create a component: 1) a new file in src/ (Greeting.jsx) with a function that returns JSX, ending with export default Greeting; 2) import it where needed: import Greeting from './Greeting.jsx'; 3) use it like an HTML tag: <Greeting name="Sonsoles" />. To render multiple components use array.map(); give each one a key prop, which is required when rendering lists and helps React track which item changed. React Developer Tools: a browser extension (Chrome Web Store, Firefox Add-ons). Open the app, press F12 and look for the new Components tab. It shows the component tree, which components are rendered, and (click a component) the props it received and its current state; you can edit values live. When something does not look right: open DevTools, find the component, check what it received and rendered, compare with what you expected.

learn.title: Props
learn.text: Props are the properties of each instance of a component: the creation parameters, provided as attributes at rendering time. They can be any type (string, number, boolean, object, function). Props are IMMUTABLE (read-only): a component never modifies its own props. Different instances of the same component can have different values, which makes components reusable. Defaults and optional values: destructure with defaults, function PostCard({ title, caption, likes = 0, imageUrl = null }), and render the image only if imageUrl is provided: {imageUrl && }.

learn.title: Callback props: events flow up
learn.text: Props can also be functions: callback props. They are used when a child component needs to notify the parent. This is one-way data binding in practice: data flows DOWN (title, id), events flow UP (the onDelete callback). The parent passes a function down as a prop, the child calls it when something happens, and the parent decides what to do with the event.

learn.title: State and useState
learn.text: State is information that changes over time: extra information that is not provided at rendering time but created and updated by the component; useful for keeping information between renderings. State is mutable but cannot be modified directly. The main feature: the component is re-rendered (repainted) each time the state changes. Application state: data you would save in a database or send/retrieve from an API (gameplay status, shopping cart), normally the state of the root <App/>. Component state: needed for UI aspects you don't save anywhere (accordion open/closed, dropdown shown/hidden, unsaved form fields). Hooks are functions that let you 'hook' into React state and lifecycle from function components; the most used are useState and useEffect. useState(initial) returns a pair [state, setter]: the first is the state, the second a function that updates it; the argument is the initial state (used for the first render). State must be updated through the setter: count = count + 1 changes a JavaScript variable but React does not know, so the UI never updates; setCount(count + 1) makes React store the new value, schedule a re-render and show it. For objects, copy with the spread operator: setCat({ ...cat, isAsleep: !cat.isAsleep }).

learn.title: Where state lives, and lifting state up
learn.text: Rule: state belongs to the LOWEST COMMON ANCESTOR of all components that need it. Does only one component need the data? Then it is component state in that component. Do multiple components need the same data? Lift the state up to their common parent. Kažigram: the posts list is needed by PostList AND PostForm, so it lives in App (the common parent); the form input text is needed only by PostForm while typing, so it lives in PostForm; the like count could live in LikeButton or Post, or in App if persisted. Lifting state up: PostForm calls props.onAddPost(newPost) (the event flows up), App updates its state, re-renders, and PostList gets the new posts (data flows down).

learn.title: Events and controlled forms
learn.text: In vanilla JS: btn.addEventListener('click', handleClick). In JSX the event handler is a prop directly on the element: <button onClick={handleClick}>. Common event props: onClick, onChange (input value changed), onSubmit (form submitted), onMouseOver. They are camelCase (onClick, not onclick). Pass the function REFERENCE, not a call: onClick={handleClick} is correct; onClick={handleClick()} calls it immediately. The cycle: user clicks, onClick calls setCount(count + 1), React stores the new value, re-renders, the UI shows the update. UI = f(state): you describe what the UI looks like for any given state, and React decides when and what to update. One state update re-renders all dependents (Header, PostList, Sidebar), while in plain JS you must update each one manually. CONTROLLED FORMS: in plain HTML the browser stores the input value and you read it on submit. In React (controlled component) state owns the value: <input value={name} onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)} />. The user types, onChange fires with an event object e, e.target is the input element, e.target.value is what was typed, setName updates the state, React re-renders and the input shows the new value. value={name} means 'always show what is in state'; without it the input is 'uncontrolled'.
learn.code:
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>      // correct: reference
<button onClick={handleClick()}>Click me</button>    // wrong: runs immediately

const [name, setName] = useState("");

const [cat, setCat] = useState("");

learn.title: useEffect: side effects
learn.text: useState stores data that changes (like count, form input, toggle); when state changes the component re-renders. useEffect runs code at specific moments in the lifecycle: 'do something WHEN something changes' or 'do something ONCE when the component appears' (update the page title, fetch data, set a timer). A side effect is anything that reaches outside React's rendering: changing the browser (document.title, localStorage), a timer or subscription, fetching data from a server. The dependency array: useEffect(fn) with no array runs after EVERY render; useEffect(fn, []) runs only ONCE when the component first appears; useEffect(fn, [count]) runs when count changes. In practice almost always include [] because it prevents infinite loops. Fetch example: the effect reaches OUTSIDE React to a server, then setPosts(data) brings the data back in and triggers a re-render. useState stores data, React manages the UI; useEffect runs code.

questions.q: What is the relationship between the Internet and the Web?
options: The Internet is the network infrastructure; the Web is one application that runs on top of it.
They are two names for the same thing.
The Web is the physical network; the Internet is a collection of websites.
The Internet is a browser; the Web is a search engine.

questions.q: How did the Web of the 1990s work?
options: Static pages were served, and every request refreshed the complete page; all logic was on the server.

JavaScript fetched small pieces of data without reloading the page.
Pages were generated in the browser from JSON delivered by WebSockets.
questions.why: That is the early static Web. Fetching pieces without reloading is AJAX (2000s); logic on the client is the SPA of today.

questions.q: What did AJAX (XMLHttpRequest) make possible?
options: Fetching pieces of a page from the server without reloading the whole page.
Storing data in the browser permanently.
Writing the server logic in HTML.
Encrypting the connection between client and server.
questions.why: AJAX = JavaScript communicating asynchronously with the server, so only part of the page updates.

questions.q: In a Single Page Application (SPA), where does most of the logic run?
questions.why: The browser fetches the app once; the server mainly stores data and handles authentication.

questions.q: Late-1990s dynamic websites were typically built how?
options: Pages generated on the server for each request (e.g. PHP or ASP), using cookies and databases for personalization.
Static HTML files only, identical for every user.
As Single Page Applications with no server code.
With native mobile apps instead of browsers.
questions.why: Each interaction still caused a full page reload, but the content became personalized.

The server never sends a response.
Only static pages can be served.
The client must stay connected for the whole session.
questions.why: Request and response are independent, though related, transmissions.
