align-items: center centres them on the cross axis (vertically)
max-width + margin: 0 auto centres a block that is at most 800px wide
nav ul is a descendant selector; list-style none removes the bullets; display:flex puts the li items in a row with a gap
nav a:hover is a pseudo-class: the link colour changes while the mouse is over it
questions.model: nav becomes a flex container, so its children (the brand link and the ul) are laid out in a row: justify-content: space-between pushes them to the two ends along the main axis and align-items: center centres them on the cross axis. max-width: 800px with margin: 0 auto makes the nav at most 800px wide and centred horizontally. 'nav ul' is a descendant selector: the bullets are removed (list-style: none) and the list is itself a flex container so the menu items are in a row with a 1.5rem gap. nav a:hover uses the :hover pseudo-class so a link changes colour while the mouse is over it.

questions.q: Explain this media query. What does it do, and what must the HTML contain for it to work properly?
keyPoints: media queries apply CSS only when a condition is true: here on screens up to 600px wide (e.g. phones)
on narrow screens the nav items stack in a column instead of a row
images in articles get a smaller height (300px)
this is responsive design: layout adapts to the screen size
the HTML needs <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
questions.model: A media query applies its rules only when a condition is true: here when the screen viewport is 600px wide or narrower, e.g. a phone. In that case the nav switches from a row to a column with a gap, and the images in articles become shorter (300px). It is responsive design: the layout adapts to the screen size. It only works correctly on mobile if the HTML head contains the viewport meta tag: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">.

questions.q: You type https://example.com/cat.html in your browser. Describe what happens between the client and the server, including HTTP method and status codes.
questions.code:
Browser  -->  GET /cat.html  -->  Server
Browser  <--  200 OK + text/html  <--  Server
keyPoints: the browser is the client and always starts the transaction by sending an HTTP request
the method is GET: read a resource from the server
the server (e.g. Apache/Nginx, listening on a port, 80 by default) answers with a response
200 OK means success and the HTML (MIME type text/html) is returned in the response
if the file does not exist the server answers 404 Not Found (4xx = client error); a server fault would be 500
HTTP is stateless: request and response are independent; the browser then fetches linked CSS/images with more requests
questions.model: The browser is the client, and the client always starts an HTTP transaction. It sends a GET request (GET = read a resource) for /cat.html to the web server (a program such as Apache or Nginx on a machine whose DNS name resolves to an IP, listening on a port, 80 by default). The server answers with a response: status 200 OK (success) and the HTML file with MIME type text/html. If the file doesn't exist the answer is 404 Not Found (a 4xx client error); if the server itself fails it is 500. HTTP is stateless, so each request/response is independent: the browser then makes further requests for the CSS, images and other files the HTML links to.

questions.q: What problem does version control solve?
options: Multiple copies of a project in different files, and overwriting files with no history
questions.why: It keeps a clear history of all changes, so nothing is lost or overwritten without a trace.

questions.q: Who created Git, and why?
options: Linus Torvalds, in 2005, to manage the development of the Linux kernel
Tim Berners-Lee, in 1989, to build the Web
GitHub, in 2008, to host open-source code
Microsoft, in 2015, for Visual Studio Code
questions.why: Git is a tool; GitHub is a separate platform built around it.

questions.q: What physically makes a project folder a Git repository?
options: A hidden .git/ folder inside the project
questions.why: git init creates the .git/ folder, which stores the history.

questions.q: Which command turns an existing folder into a Git repository?
questions.why: git init creates the repository. git clone copies an existing one.

questions.q: Which command shows the state of the working directory and staging area?
questions.why: git status is the first thing to run when something seems wrong.

questions.q: Which command moves changes to the staging area?
questions.why: add = working directory to staging; commit = staging to local repository; push = local to remote.

questions.q: What does  git commit -m "First version"  do?
options: Saves a snapshot of all staged changes in the local repository with that message
Stages all files in the folder
Creates a new branch called First version
questions.why: Committing does not touch the remote. You need git push for that.

questions.q: Which command shows your commit history, one line per commit?
questions.why: Each commit has a unique identifier (SHA-1).

questions.q: What is the staging area?
options: Where you prepare the changes for the next commit
The folder where you edit files
The place where committed snapshots are stored
questions.why: Working directory = edit files. Staging = prepare next commit. Local repository = committed code. Remote = server for sharing.

questions.q: Which area holds the code that HAS been committed?
questions.why: The Git directory stores committed snapshots.

questions.q: What makes a good commit message?
options: It describes what was changed and why
It contains the whole source code
questions.why: Messages help you identify a specific version later. Conventions such as 'chore: ignore node_modules' help too.

questions.q: What is a .gitignore file for?
options: Listing files that Git should not track
questions.why: Example contents: *.pem, *.log, passwords.txt.

questions.q: A file is already tracked by Git. You now add it to .gitignore. What happens?
options: Nothing changes: it is still tracked, and you must untrack it manually (git rm --cached)
Git automatically deletes it from the repository
questions.why: That is why .gitignore should be set up BEFORE the first commit.

questions.q: What does  git add .  do?
options: Stages all files in the directory (including ones you may not want, unless ignored)
questions.why: Be careful: that is why you create .gitignore first.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of the basic local workflow?
options: git init, git add, git commit
git commit, git add, git init
git add, git init, git push
git push, git commit, git add
questions.why: Initialize, stage, commit (then push if you have a remote).

questions.q: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
options: Git is the version control tool used locally; GitHub is a cloud platform for hosting repositories and collaboration
GitHub is the tool; Git is the website
Git hosts websites; GitHub tracks changes
questions.why: Alternatives to GitHub: GitLab, Bitbucket, Codeberg.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a platform for hosting Git repositories?
questions.why: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Codeberg are hosting platforms.

questions.q: What does  git config --global user.name "Your Name"  set?
options: The author name used on your commits, for all projects of your user
questions.why: Priority: --local (this project) overrides --global (your user), which overrides --system.

questions.q: You set a different user.name with --local inside one project. Which name is used in that project?
questions.why: Priority: local, then global, then system.

questions.q: What does  git remote add origin <url>  do?
options: Links the local project to a remote repository named origin
questions.why: After that, git push and git pull synchronize local and remote.

questions.q: What does git push do?
options: Sends committed changes from your current branch to the remote repository
questions.why: push = local to remote. pull = remote to local.

questions.q: git pull is equal to which two commands?
questions.why: fetch downloads remote changes without changing your working files; pull fetches and then merges.

questions.q: What does git fetch do?
options: Downloads remote changes without changing your working files
Sends your commits to the remote
questions.why: pull = fetch + merge.

questions.q: Which command downloads an existing repository from GitHub to your computer?
questions.why: clone makes a local copy. fork is a GitHub feature that makes a remote copy.

questions.q: Which command moves a file back from the staging area to the working directory (unstages it)?
questions.why: git restore is for restoring files; git switch is for branches.

questions.q: What does GitHub Pages do?
options: Makes the files in a repository available as a webpage (myuser.github.io/myrepository)
questions.why: It publishes your site instead of showing just the files.

questions.q: What is a Git tag?
options: A name that marks a specific commit as a version (e.g. v1-html)
A kind of branch that merges itself
A comment on a pull request
questions.why: Create: git tag v1-html. Push: git push origin v1-html. List: git tag.

questions.q: What is a GitHub Release?
options: A tag plus a description and downloadable files
questions.why: Users can download a release as a ZIP without needing Git.

questions.q: Where do you add collaborators to your repository on GitHub?
questions.why: They accept the invitation, then clone the repository (Exercise 2, step 3).

questions.q: Why use branches?
options: Isolated feature work that is safer than working directly on main, and collaboration without overwriting each other's work
questions.why: When the feature is ready, merge it back to main.

questions.q: Which command creates a new branch AND switches to it?
questions.why: git branch name only creates it; git switch name only switches.

questions.q: Which command lists the existing branches?
questions.why: git branch name creates one; git branch -d name deletes one.

questions.q: Which command deletes a branch (clean up after merging)?
questions.why: -d = delete.

questions.q: What is the difference between git switch, git restore and git checkout?
options: switch handles branches, restore handles files, and the older checkout does both
They are three names for exactly the same command
switch deletes branches, restore creates them, checkout merges them
checkout is the newest of the three
questions.why: Modern Git (2.23+) split checkout into switch and restore. switch is clearer because it only handles branch switching.

questions.q: You finished work on the branch add-image. What do you do to merge it into main?
options: git switch main, then git merge add-image
git switch add-image, then git merge main
questions.why: You merge INTO the branch you are currently on, so switch to main first.

questions.q: In Exercise 2, why does step 5 cause a merge conflict while step 4 does not?
options: In step 5 everyone changes the same line (<title>) differently; in step 4 people change different parts of the file
In step 5 the branches have the same name
questions.why: A conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines in the same file differently.

questions.q: What is the difference between clone and fork?
options: clone makes a local copy on your computer; fork makes a remote copy under your own GitHub account
clone makes a copy on GitHub; fork makes a copy on your computer
They are the same; fork is the older name
clone is only for public repos; fork is only for private ones
questions.why: Remember: clone = to my computer, fork = to my GitHub account.

questions.q: When should you FORK a repository instead of just cloning it?
options: You don't have permission to push to the original and want to contribute via a pull request
You want a local working copy of your own repo
You want to delete the original
You want to avoid using GitHub
questions.why: Fork gives you your own writable copy on GitHub.

questions.q: Which is the correct pull request workflow?
options: fork, clone, branch, commit & push, pull request, review, merge
clone, merge, fork, branch, review, push
branch, fork, merge, clone, commit, pull request
pull request, fork, commit, merge, branch, clone
questions.why: You push to your fork, then open a pull request against the original repo; maintainers review and merge.

questions.q: What is a pull request?
options: A request to the maintainers to review and merge your changes into the original repository
A command that downloads changes (same as git pull)
A request to delete a branch
A way to copy a repository to your computer
questions.why: Maintainers can comment and request modifications before merging.

questions.q: Something goes wrong in Git. What is the first thing to do?
options: Delete the local repository and clone again
questions.why: Then identify your branch and ask whether the problem is local, branch-related or remote. Read the error message carefully.

questions.q: Why does a merge conflict happen?
options: Two branches changed the same lines in the same file differently, and Git cannot decide which to keep
The branch name is too long
questions.why: Conflicts are normal in collaborative work.

questions.q: Which markers appear in a file with a merge conflict?
questions.why: <<<<<<< HEAD starts your version, ======= separates, >>>>>>> branch_name ends the other version.

questions.q: What are the steps to resolve a merge conflict?
options: git status, open the file, choose or combine versions, remove all markers, save, git add the file, git commit
Delete the repository and clone again
Rename the branch and merge again
questions.why: Do not leave conflict markers in the file; Git won't complete the merge.

questions.q: Your push is rejected: 'Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally'. What do you do?
options: git pull, resolve conflicts if they appear, then git push
Delete your local repo and start over
questions.why: Someone else pushed first (or you edited on GitHub), so your branch is behind. Force-pushing could delete others' work.

questions.q: Why is git push --force dangerous?
options: It can overwrite the remote and delete other people's work
questions.why: Don't force-push or delete anything unless you know why.

questions.q: You committed to main by mistake but have NOT pushed. Which sequence fixes it?
options: git reset --soft HEAD~1, git stash, git switch correct-branch, git stash pop, git add ., git commit
git revert, then git reset --hard origin
questions.why: reset --soft undoes the commit but keeps the changes staged; stash carries them to the right branch.

questions.q: What does  git reset --soft HEAD~1  do?
options: Undoes the last commit; the changes stay in the staging area
Deletes the last commit and the changes
questions.why: HEAD~1 means one commit back.

questions.q: You committed to the wrong branch AND already pushed. What is the recommended fix?
options: Create a new branch from the current state and push it, switch to main, then git revert the wrong commit and push
git push --force to rewrite the history
questions.why: git revert undoes the commit safely with a new commit; force-pushing rewrites shared history.

questions.q: What is 'detached HEAD'?
options: You checked out a specific commit instead of a branch, so you are not on any branch
questions.why: Commits made there can become 'lost' unless you create a branch first.

questions.q: You are in detached HEAD and want to KEEP the changes you made. What do you do?
questions.why: If you only wanted to look at the old version, git switch main returns you to the branch.

questions.q: You accidentally committed node_modules/. Which command stops tracking it while keeping it on your computer?
questions.why: Then add it to .gitignore, git add .gitignore, git commit, git push. Just deleting it locally is not enough: Git still tracks it.

questions.q: You accidentally pushed a file containing an API key. What must you do first?
options: Rotate the key immediately (change it), because the old one is exposed in history
Make the repository private and do nothing else
questions.why: Even after cleanup the file is still in Git history. A changed key makes the old one useless.

questions.q: Push fails with 'Support for password authentication was removed'. Which are valid fixes?
options: A Personal Access Token, SSH keys, or VS Code's Source Control panel
questions.why: GitHub no longer accepts your account password for Git operations. Never commit tokens or keys.

questions.q: Which statement about conflict markers is correct?
options: You must remove all of them before committing the resolution
You can leave them in the file
questions.why: If markers are left, the merge will not be completed correctly.

questions.q: Explain what each command does and which area of Git it moves changes between.
questions.code:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "First version"
git remote add origin https://github.com/you/repo.git
git push -u origin main
keyPoints: git init makes the folder a Git repository (creates the .git folder)
git add . moves all changes from the working directory to the staging area
git commit saves a snapshot of the staged changes to the local repository, with a message
git remote add origin links the local project to the GitHub repository
git push sends the committed changes of the current branch (main) to the remote repository
the three areas plus remote: working directory, staging area, local repository, remote repository
questions.model: git init turns the folder into a Git repository by creating the .git folder. git add . moves all my changes from the working directory to the staging area, where I prepare the next commit. git commit -m saves a snapshot of everything staged into the local repository, with a message that says what/why. git remote add origin <url> links this local project to a repository on GitHub (the remote). git push -u origin main sends the committed changes of my main branch from the local repository to the remote, so they are shared and backed up.

questions.q: This file appears after a merge. What happened, why, and how do you finish the merge?
questions.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
<title>Sherlock</title>
=======
<title>Holmes</title>
>>>>>>> add-title
keyPoints: it is a merge conflict: two branches changed the same line (the title) differently
Git cannot decide which version to keep, so it stops and marks both
the part between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is the current branch's version; the part after ======= is the add-title branch's version
open the file, choose one version or combine them, and remove all the markers
save, git add the file, then git commit to complete the merge
git status shows which files have conflicts; do not force-push
questions.model: This is a merge conflict. Two branches changed the same line (the <title>) in different ways, so Git cannot decide which to keep and stopped the merge, marking both versions. Between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is the version on my current branch; between ======= and >>>>>>> add-title is the version from the add-title branch. To resolve: use git status to see the conflicted files, open the file, decide which version to keep (or combine them), delete all the marker lines, save, git add the file and git commit (e.g. "resolve merge conflict"). I should not force-push; conflicts are normal in collaboration.

questions.q: Describe the workflow in this code and explain why branches are used.
questions.code:
git switch -c add-image
# ... edit index.html ...
git add .
git commit -m "Add real image and alt text"
git switch main
git merge add-image
git push
keyPoints: git switch -c creates a new branch add-image and switches to it
the work is committed on the branch, isolated from main
git switch main goes back to main, and git merge add-image brings the feature into main (you merge into the branch you are on)
git push shares the updated main with the remote
branches give isolated feature work, are safer than working directly on main, and let several people work without overwriting each other
questions.model: git switch -c add-image creates a new branch and switches to it. I edit files and commit there, so the change is isolated and main stays safe. When the feature is ready I switch back to main and run git merge add-image, which merges the feature branch into the branch I am on (main). git push then shares main with the remote repository. Branches are used for isolated feature work: it is safer than editing main directly, and several collaborators can work at the same time without overwriting each other's work.

questions.q: You run git push and get: "! [rejected] main -> main (non-fast-forward) ... the remote contains work that you do not have locally". Why did this happen and what should you do?
questions.code:
$ git push
! [rejected]        main -> main (non-fast-forward)
error: failed to push some refs
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains
hint: work that you do not have locally.
keyPoints: someone else pushed to the same branch first (or changes were made directly on GitHub), so the local branch is behind the remote
run git pull (fetch + merge) to get the remote changes
resolve any merge conflicts that appear, then commit
then git push again
do not use git push --force or delete the local repository: that could destroy others' work
questions.model: The push was rejected because my local main is behind the remote: someone else pushed to the same branch before me (or someone edited on GitHub directly), so the remote contains commits I do not have locally. I should run git pull, which fetches the remote changes and merges them; if there are merge conflicts I resolve them and commit; then git push works. I should not use git push --force or delete my local repo and start over, because that could overwrite or lose other people's work.

questions.q: You want to contribute a fix to an open-source project you do not have write access to. Explain the steps and the difference between clone and fork.
questions.code: fork -> clone -> branch -> commit & push -> pull request -> review -> merge
keyPoints: fork the project to your own GitHub account (a remote copy you can write to)
clone your fork to your computer (a local copy)
create a branch for your changes, commit, and push to your fork
open a pull request against the original repository
maintainers review, discuss, may request changes, and then merge
clone copies a repo to your computer; fork copies it to your own GitHub account; you fork because you cannot push to the original
questions.model: Because I cannot push to the original repository, I fork it: that makes my own remote copy under my GitHub account. Then I clone my fork to my computer, create a branch for the fix, commit, and push the branch to my fork. Then I open a pull request against the original repository. The maintainers review and discuss it, may ask for changes, and then merge it. The difference: clone copies a repository to my computer (a local copy), while fork makes a remote copy of someone's repository under my own GitHub account.

questions.q: What does web accessibility mean?
options: Making websites usable for all people, including those with disabilities
Making websites available only on mobile
questions.why: Disabilities can be visual, auditory, motor or cognitive.

questions.q: Which kinds of disabilities does accessible design consider?
questions.why: Accessible design benefits everyone, not only people with disabilities.

questions.q: Which is an example of how accessible design helps everyone?
options: Better colour contrast helps when reading a phone in bright sunlight
questions.why: Other examples: captions in noisy environments, keyboard navigation for those who prefer keyboards.

questions.q: What does WCAG stand for?
questions.why: WCAG and the EU accessibility act are legal/standard references for accessibility.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the reasons accessibility matters (according to the lecture)?
options: It makes the page run faster on the server
Social responsibility: equal access to information and services
Practical benefits: usability, SEO and user experience
questions.why: Legal, social and practical reasons. SEO = search engine optimization.

questions.q: What are the four principles of accessible design (POUR)?
questions.why: Perceivable = visible/audible; Operable = mouse/keyboard/assistive tech; Understandable = clear; Robust = works with different devices and assistive technologies.

questions.q: Which POUR principle says that users must be able to navigate with a mouse, a keyboard or assistive technology?
questions.why: Perceivable: seen/heard. Understandable: clear content. Robust: works across devices and assistive tech.

questions.q: Which POUR principle does adding alt text to an image mainly support?
questions.why: Alt text makes the image information available to people who cannot see it (screen readers).

questions.q: Which of these is an accessibility feature?
options: Low contrast between text and background
Removing alt text to reduce page size
questions.why: Other features: alt text, high contrast, keyboard navigation.

questions.q: What does ARIA stand for?
questions.why: ARIA is a set of HTML attributes for assistive technologies.

questions.q: What do ARIA attributes do?
options: Add extra meaning for assistive software such as screen readers, without changing how the page looks
Change the colours of the page
questions.why: Example: <button aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="menu1">.

questions.q: What are UI elements (components)?
options: The building blocks of apps and websites that users interact with
The server-side code of a website
The images used in a website
questions.why: Examples: buttons, navbars, cards, forms, modals.

questions.q: What does UX stand for and mean?
options: User eXperience: how users experience a product
User eXchange: how data is exchanged
questions.why: UI = the interface elements, UX = the experience of using them.

questions.q: Why do designers reuse well-known UI components?
options: Familiar patterns build user trust and keep experiences predictable; breaking patterns confuses users
Because it is illegal to design new ones
Because browsers only support a few components
questions.why: That is why the same components appear across many websites.

questions.q: What is a UI component library?
options: A collection of reusable components guided by clear standards
questions.why: Purpose: consistency, scalability and efficiency in web development.

questions.q: Why is a UI component library useful?
options: Consistency, scalability and efficiency in web development
It replaces the need for HTML
It removes the need for a browser
questions.why: You reuse ready-made, standardised components instead of building everything from scratch.

questions.q: What is Bootstrap?
options: An open-source CSS framework with ready-made HTML, CSS and JavaScript components for responsive, mobile-first sites
A JavaScript library for fetching data
questions.why: It is free and very widely used.

questions.q: What does 'mobile-first' mean for Bootstrap?
options: Layouts are designed for small screens first, and larger breakpoints add changes
It loads faster on phones only
questions.why: That is why col-12 (full width) is the default and col-lg-* adds the desktop layout.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of using a framework like Bootstrap?
options: Speeds up development and makes responsive design easy
It removes the need for accessibility
questions.why: Also: built-in components, consistency across devices and browsers, large community and documentation.

questions.q: How can you add Bootstrap to a project?
options: With a CDN link, or by downloading it and including it locally
Only by writing all the CSS yourself
questions.why: The CDN <link> goes in the head.

questions.q: How do you use Bootstrap on an element?
options: By adding Bootstrap's predefined CSS classes to the HTML element
By writing JavaScript for every element
By using inline style attributes only
questions.why: Example: <button class="btn btn-primary">. Each class applies a set of CSS rules; combine classes to get the look.

questions.q:
What does

do?

questions.q: What does  class="btn btn-primary"  produce?
options: A button styled with Bootstrap's primary colour
questions.why: btn is the base button class and btn-primary the colour variant.

questions.q: How many columns does the Bootstrap grid have?
questions.why: A row is divided into 12 columns; classes say how many a column takes.

questions.q: Which structure does the Bootstrap grid use?
questions.why: <div class="container"><div class="row"><div class="col-md-6">…

One third on small screens; full width on large screens
questions.why: col-12 = all 12 columns (stacked on mobile); col-lg-4 = 4/12 at 992px and up.

.container spans the full width; .container-fluid is fixed width

questions.why: Classes: breadcrumb (list), breadcrumb-item (each level), active (current page). CSS adds the separators.

questions.q: Compare callbacks, Promises and async/await for handling asynchronous code. Which is the modern standard and why?

questions.model: Callbacks are functions passed as arguments and called when the task is done; for several steps they become deeply nested, hard to read and debug, and the error handling must be repeated at every level. Promises represent the eventual result of an async operation (pending, then fulfilled or rejected) and give a flat .then() chain with a single .catch() for all errors, but when a step needs data from an earlier step you have to keep it in outer variables. async/await is built on Promises and reads like normal sequential code: all variables stay in the same scope, and one try/catch handles all errors. That is why it is the modern standard.

questions.q: Explain what a REST API is and how a web page uses one. Cover resources, HTTP methods, the data format and statelessness.

the data is a resource identified by a URL; the HTTP method defines the action: GET = read, POST = create, PUT = update, DELETE = remove
responses are typically JSON, lighter than XML and compatible with JavaScript objects
stateless: each request is independent and contains everything the server needs (e.g. an API key); the server remembers nothing between requests
in JavaScript we use fetch with async/await, then use the data to update the DOM
questions.model: A REST API is an address (URL) provided by another server. Our JavaScript sends an HTTP request to it, the server processes it and responds with data, usually in JSON, which we then use to update the DOM. Data is treated as a resource identified by its URL, and the HTTP method says what to do with it: GET to read, POST to create, PUT to update, DELETE to remove. JSON is preferred over XML because it is lighter and directly compatible with JavaScript objects. REST is stateless: every request must be independent and contain all the information the server needs (that is why an API key is sent in every request), and the server does not remember previous requests. In JavaScript we call it with fetch using async/await, because waiting for the server takes time.

questions.model: The posts state lives in App because both PostList and PostForm need it, and state belongs to the lowest common ancestor of the components that need it: this is lifting state up. App passes posts down to PostList as a prop, so data flows down. It passes the function addPost down to PostForm as the callback prop onAddPost. When the form is submitted, PostForm calls props.onAddPost(newPost): the event flows up. addPost calls setPosts with a new array made with the spread operator ([...posts, newPost]), which copies the old posts and adds the new one. React re-renders, and PostList receives the new posts and shows the new post.

questions.model: Fetching data from a server is a side effect: it reaches outside React's rendering, so it is put in useEffect, which runs after the render. The posts state starts as an empty array so the component can render before the data arrives. Inside the effect an async function awaits fetch and then res.json(), because both are asynchronous. setPosts(data) brings the fetched data into state, which triggers a re-render that shows the posts. The empty dependency array [] means the effect runs only once, when the component first appears; without it, the effect would run after every render, and setting state would cause an infinite loop. Finally map renders one PostCard per post, with a key.

questions.model: I would read the requirements and find repeating patterns: every post looks the same, so PostCard is a component, rendered many times by PostList. App is the root component. There is a Header with navigation, a PostForm for adding a post, and a LikeButton and DeleteButton inside each PostCard. Props: PostCard receives the post object (title, caption, photo, like count) and callback props such as onDelete. State: the posts array is application state and lives in App, the lowest common ancestor of PostList and PostForm; the form's input values are component state inside PostForm. Data flows down through props and events flow up through callbacks, which is one-way data binding. The like count is App state if it has to be saved, or component state if it is only visual feedback. There is no single right answer; the design decisions matter.

questions.q: Why was React created, and how does it differ from manipulating the DOM directly? Mention the Virtual DOM.
keyPoints: as apps grow, direct DOM manipulation becomes 'DOM spaghetti': scattered state, duplicated code, hard to track what to update
React lets you split the UI into reusable components that take props and return UI
with React the developer describes what the UI should look like; React works out how to update the DOM
Virtual DOM: React compares the new Virtual DOM with the previous one (diffing) and updates only the necessary parts of the real DOM
one-way data binding makes data flow predictable: data down, events up
questions.model: As apps grow, manipulating the DOM directly with getElementById and addEventListener turns into 'DOM spaghetti': state is scattered, code is duplicated and it is hard to track which parts to update. React solves this by letting you split the UI into reusable components that take props and return UI. With React the developer describes what the UI should look like and React works out how to update the page: it keeps a Virtual DOM, compares the new one with the previous one (diffing) and updates only the parts of the real DOM that changed. Its one-way data binding (data flows down through props, events flow up through callbacks) makes the data flow predictable and easier to debug.

It receives props name, age, imageUrl, x and y and builds a style object from them: position absolute, left and top set from x and y (with 'px'), centered text, and imageRendering 'pixelated'. The object is given to the div's style attribute (camelCase property names). Inside the div it shows the image at 120px wide and, below it, a paragraph with the name and age. Each use of <Creature /> with different props appears at a different position as a pixel-art creature with its caption, and pixelated rendering stops the browser blurring the small image when it is scaled up.

questions.model: CreatureField is the parent. Its div has position relative and a fixed width and height, so the absolutely positioned Creature children are placed relative to it and stay inside the field. Each Creature is given different props (name, age, imageUrl, x, y), so data flows down from parent to child and each one appears with its own information at its own position, without overlapping. In the bonus version the creatures would be an array of objects in CreatureField, rendered with creatures.map(c => <Creature key={c.name} ... />) so the five repeated tags become one expression, and each element needs a unique key.
